findings.plain: The paper counts how many patients had one, two, three, or more heart-and-circulation conditions, then lists the ten commonest combinations at each level. At the "two conditions" level the ten listed pairs cover more than twice as many patients as the paper says had two conditions at all, and at the "three conditions" level they cover about 40% more than it says had three. The list of one-condition patients in the very same table behaves correctly, which is what makes the other two stand out: either those numbers are wrong, or the table quietly switches to counting patients a different way partway down without telling the reader. This affects the paper's descriptions of how conditions cluster together; it does not touch the statistical comparisons in Tables 2 and 3.

consequence.explanation: Affects the Results claims that 470 patients (16.60%) had two comorbidities, that primary hypertension plus sequelae of cerebrovascular disease was the commonest pair at 6.71%, and that 8.66% had three conditions; no test statistic in Table 2 or coefficient in Table 3 is computed from these blocks.

findings.plain: The four patient groups the paper discovers are almost the same thing as the three hospitals the data came from: 369 of the 375 patients in the "heart failure" group come from one region, and 224 of the 225 in the "cardiac valve" group come from the other. That means a finding like "perphenazine is strongly linked to heart failure" cannot be separated from "the hospital that prescribes perphenazine is the hospital whose records produce the heart-failure group". Putting region into the model does not fix this, because region and group membership are so nearly identical that the model cannot tell them apart -- which is exactly what the printed odds ratio of 0.00 for region is reporting. The paper does not raise this as a limitation.

consequence.explanation: Bears directly on the abstract's headline medication claims -- perphenazine (OR = 22.06) and chlorpromazine hydrochloride (OR = 7.09) "strongly linked to comorbid heart failure" -- because membership in the heart-failure class is close to equivalent to being treated at the Southwest sites, whose formularies are not reported.

findings.title: Abstract class prevalences irreconcilable with the class sizes every reported test was computed on
findings.location: Abstract and Results "Proportion of diseases and comorbidity patterns", against the Table 2 column headers
findings.reported: Abstract: "four distinct comorbidity patterns were identified ... low-risk CVDs (47.86%), primary hypertension (30.15%), heart failure (12.99%), and cardiac valve and vascular disorders (8.99%)". Table 2 column headers give the class sizes used for every chi-squared test and every regression coefficient as n = 1293, 937, 375 and 225 out of N = 2830.
findings.computed: A GRIM sweep over n in [2700, 2900] finds no sample size at which all four percentages can simultaneously be whole-number counts, and n = 2830 appears in none of the four individual viability lists. At denominators near 2830 the percentages correspond to roughly 1354, 853, 368 and 254 patients, against Table 2's 1293, 937, 375 and 225. The largest gap is the cardiac-valve class, where the abstract's 8.99% implies about 254 patients against the 225 actually analysed.
findings.assumptions: This is a REINTERPRETATION, not an impossibility claim: the tool returns `impossible` for the question it was asked (can these four share a denominator?), and the answer being no is the expected and legitimate behaviour of latent class analysis, whose estimated mixing proportions are not headcounts and need not divide N. Severity therefore reflects reporting transparency, not arithmetic error, and no R cross-check is required because no impossibility is being asserted. The sweep range 2700-2900 was chosen by this review to bracket the stated N = 2830; the finding does not depend on that choice, since 2830 itself is absent from every list.
findings.reproduction: metascience grim-sweep --values '[47.86,30.15,12.99,8.99]' --n-min 2700 --n-max 2900 --decimals 2 --value-type percentage    # if the CLI verb name differs, the equivalent MCP call is grim_sweep(values=[47.86,30.15,12.99,8.99], n_min=2700, n_max=2900, decimals=2, value_type='percentage'); this review invoked it via MCP and did not confirm the CLI spelling
findings.plain: The abstract gives four headline figures for how common each comorbidity pattern is -- 47.86%, 30.15%, 12.99%, 8.99%. None of these can be a percentage of the 2,830 patients studied; they are a by-product of the statistical model rather than a count of people. The actual group sizes used in every test the paper reports are 1,293, 937, 375 and 225, and for the smallest group the abstract's figure overstates the number of patients by roughly 13%. This is a normal quirk of the method used, but the paper never says which number is which, and the abstract's figures are the ones a reader will take away as prevalence.

consequence.explanation: Affects the four prevalence figures in the abstract and repeated in the Results, which do not correspond to the class sizes on which every chi-squared test in Table 2 and every coefficient in Table 3 was computed.

not_checked.reason: statcheck ran successfully and found zero statistics to verify. This is a property of the paper's reporting style rather than a tool failure: the chi-squared values in Table 2 are printed without degrees of freedom and with asterisk markers instead of p-values, and the regression results are given as bare odds ratios with no test statistic, so none of it matches the APA grammar statcheck parses. The chi-squared verification in this review came instead from recomputing each statistic from its own contingency table, which is a stronger check.

not_checked.location: Multiplicity correction arithmetic over the Table 3 coefficient family
not_checked.reason: multiplicity_report returned n_tests = 0 on all attempts across both stages, under four different argument shapes. No corrected thresholds, no surviving-claim bounds and no count of claims lost to correction could be produced, so none is asserted anywhere in this report.

Not applicable. The paper reports no means with standard deviations anywhere -- Tables 1 and 2 are counts with percentages and Table 3 is odds ratios with intervals -- so there are no (mean, SD) pairs for the duplication check to compare.

Not applicable and deliberately not run. This is a cross-sectional secondary analysis of electronic medical records with no randomisation and no allocated arms; the Table 2 groups are latent classes derived from the outcome data itself, so baseline p-values carry none of the meaning they carry in a randomised trial and an excess-similarity test on them would be meaningless.

limitations: Figures were NOT read in this run. extract_figures was not called and no figure crops were produced or inspected at either stage; Fig. 1 (comorbidity network map) and Fig. 2 (latent-class conditional probabilities) were assessed only from their captions and from the summary values quoted in the body text. Fig. 2 in particular carries the per-indicator conditional probabilities for 50 diagnoses across 4 classes, which appear nowhere else in the paper, so the substance of the latent-class solution was not visually verified.

The single most consequential check in this paper -- whether four classes is the right number -- could not be run at all, because the model-selection statistics live in a supplementary spreadsheet that exceeded the extraction limit. Every result in Tables 2 and 3 is conditional on that choice.

The multiplicity arithmetic failed to execute on four separate attempts across both stages. No statement about how many of the paper's borderline associations would survive correction appears anywhere in this report, and its absence reflects our tooling rather than a finding that the family is adequately controlled.

The headline finding rests on a definitional reading of Table 1's block structure. The alternative reading -- that the binary and ternary blocks count overlapping rather than exclusive combinations -- reconciles the arithmetic and cannot be excluded from the published text alone, which is why the severity is capped below `impossible`. Only the authors or the underlying eTables 2-4 can settle it.

All numeric values were read from the publisher JATS XML. No table was flagged alignment_uncertain or image_only, and Tables 1 and 3 were re-fetched at this stage and their cells confirmed verbatim, but no independent PDF cross-check of the numbers was performed at either stage.

Table 2 was not re-fetched at this stage; the eight chi-squared verifications and 35 count-sum reconciliations reported as passing are carried over from the sweep, with only the region cross-tabulation independently re-run here.

The site confounding described in finding 2 is a design-validity judgement built on verified counts. Whether it materially changes any specific coefficient was not determined, because that would require refitting the model on data the paper does not release.

tables_checked: Table 1 (52 rows x 3 cols; 102 count/percentage values; re-fetched and verified at stage 2)
Table 2 (73 rows x 7 cols; ~300 count/percentage cells plus 8 test statistics; region cross-tabulation re-run at stage 2)
Table 3 (61 rows x 8 cols; 153 OR/CI cells and 153 p-values; re-fetched at stage 2, 21 cells checked in full)

questions_for_authors.question: Table 1's "Binary comorbidity (Top 10)" rows total 1147 patients (40.52% of the sample), and the "Ternary comorbidity (Top 10)" rows total 341 (12.06%), while the Results state that 470 patients (16.60%) had two CVD comorbidities and 8.66% had three. Are these blocks counting patients with exactly two (or exactly three) comorbidities, or every patient carrying that combination irrespective of how many other conditions they have? If the latter, could the same be confirmed or denied for the "Single comorbidity (Top 10)" block, whose 706 primary-hypertension cases sit well below the 1306 in the "Diseases of the circulatory system" block?
questions_for_authors.why: This is the headline finding and the single question that would settle it. The Single block demonstrably uses the exclusive definition; if the Binary and Ternary blocks do too, their totals cannot be right.

questions_for_authors.question: The abstract reports the four comorbidity patterns as 47.86%, 30.15%, 12.99% and 8.99%, while Table 2 gives the class sizes used in every subsequent test as n = 1293, 937, 375 and 225 of 2830. None of the four percentages is a whole-number count over 2830. Are the abstract figures the model's estimated mixing proportions rather than modal-assignment shares, and could the modal class percentages be reported alongside them?
questions_for_authors.why: Would confirm the reinterpretation and remove the reader's natural but incorrect inference that the abstract figures are prevalences of the analysed groups. The gap is largest for the cardiac-valve class (8.99% implying ~254 patients against the 225 analysed).

questions_for_authors.question: Table 2 shows 369 of the 375 heart-failure-class patients drawn from Southwest China and 224 of the 225 cardiac-valve-class patients from Northern China (chi-squared = 1140.6, df = 3). Given that two of the four latent classes are close to being site indicators, could you report the site-specific prescribing frequencies for perphenazine and chlorpromazine hydrochloride, and say whether the OR = 22.06 and OR = 7.09 associations with heart failure persist within site?
questions_for_authors.why: Directly tests whether the abstract's headline medication findings are drug effects or hospital effects. The authors already hold the site-level prescription data.

questions_for_authors.question: Five cells in the Heart failure column of Table 3 are degenerate -- notably "0.00 (0.00, 0.00)" with p < 0.001 for Northern region, "0.00 (0.00, 0.32)" for widowed patients and "1.88 (0, 31465.17)" for other anxiolytics -- and Table 2 shows the corresponding zero cells. Were penalised-likelihood (e.g. Firth) estimates considered for the heart-failure equation, and can the coefficients for the non-separated predictors in that equation be reported from such a fit?
questions_for_authors.why: Establishes whether the whole heart-failure equation is affected by quasi-complete separation or only the five printed cells, which determines how much of the heart-failure column can be relied on.

questions_for_authors.question: Table 1 lists the seven ICD-10 psychiatric categories as 2273, 324, 191, 26, 17, 5 and 4, which total 2840 against the stated N = 2830, while the accompanying percentages are each consistent with a denominator of 2830. Do ten patients carry two F20-F29 category codes, or is one of the counts a transcription error?
questions_for_authors.why: A single number would resolve it, and the inclusion criteria imply one category per patient.

questions_for_authors.question: The Results state that patients treated with lorazepam "exhibited a higher likelihood of comorbid primary hypertension (OR = 0.79)", while Table 3 gives 0.79 (0.65, 0.96), p = 0.019 and the Discussion describes a negative correlation. Should the Results sentence read "lower likelihood"?
questions_for_authors.why: A one-word correction; the table and Discussion already agree with each other.

questions_for_authors.question: Supplementary eTable 5 contains the BIC and other fit indices used to select the four-class solution. Could those values be reported in the main text or supplied as a plain CSV, together with the entropy and average class-membership probabilities for the 2- to 6-class models?
questions_for_authors.why: The four-class choice determines every result in Tables 2 and 3 and is currently the only wholly unverifiable step in the analysis; the supplementary workbook could not be read.

report_markdown:
This paper takes electronic medical records from three Chinese psychiatric hospitals over 2015-2023, selects the 2,830 inpatients with a schizophrenia-spectrum diagnosis who also had a cardiovascular condition recorded at discharge, and uses latent class analysis over 50 ICD-10 cardiovascular categories to sort them into four comorbidity patterns: low-risk, primary hypertension, heart failure, and cardiac valve and vascular disorders. It then compares the four groups on demographics and psychotropic prescribing, and fits a multinomial logistic model reporting 153 odds ratios. The headline claims are that men are more likely to fall in the hypertension and heart-failure patterns, and that perphenazine (OR = 22.06) and chlorpromazine hydrochloride (OR = 7.09) are strongly linked to comorbid heart failure.

The paper's inferential machinery is, on its own terms, in good order. All eight chi-squared statistics in Table 2 reproduce exactly from the contingency tables printed beside them -- 180.74, 900.21, 65.69, 274.90, 36.72, 473.19, 1140.6 and 20.14 all recompute to the printed precision, and the two with exact significance markers carry the right one. All 35 count sums in Table 2 reconcile with tolerance zero, and the four class sizes total 2,830. Of the 21 odds-ratio cells in Table 3 checked in full, every one sits at the log-scale midpoint of its own interval and, where an exact p is printed, agrees with the p recovered from the interval width. This is not a paper whose arithmetic collapses under recalculation.

What does not hold up is Table 1, and the reason it matters is that the table contains its own control. Three blocks list the ten commonest comorbidity combinations at one, two and three conditions. The one-condition block behaves exactly as a top-ten subset must: its 1,734 patients sit below the stated 1,893, and its 706 hypertension cases sit well below the 1,306 hypertension cases in the same table's overall disease block -- proving that block counts patients exclusively. The two- and three-condition blocks, carrying parallel headers, overshoot their stated totals by factors of 2.4 and 1.4. The percentage columns make this visible without any derivation at all: 40.52% against a stated 16.60%, and 12.06% against a stated 8.66%. One reading rescues the arithmetic -- that these rows count overlapping rather than exclusive combinations -- but it requires one table to use two incompatible definitions under matched headings, and the paper says nothing of it. That ambiguity is why this is reported as an inconsistency rather than an impossibility, and why the supplementary eTables 3 and 4 would settle it in a sentence.

The deeper problem is not arithmetic at all, and no numeric sweep would raise it on its own. Two of the four latent classes are very nearly site labels. Of 375 heart-failure-class patients, 369 are from Southwest China; of 225 cardiac-valve-class patients, 224 are from Northern China. The chi-squared of 1140.6 reproduces exactly, so this is a real feature of the data rather than a reporting error -- but it means the model cannot separate a drug effect from a hospital effect. Perphenazine and chlorpromazine are older, cheaper agents whose use varies sharply by formulary, and the class they predict is largely one region's records. The model's own output says as much: the region odds ratio for heart failure is printed as 0.00 (0.00, 0.00). That is not an estimate; it is a maximum-likelihood fit diverging under quasi-complete separation, and four other cells in the same column do the same thing, one of them spanning an interval from 0 to 31,465. The paper reports these in the same format as its well-identified estimates, with no caveat, no penalised-likelihood alternative, and two sentences in the Results that summarise them as findings about patients. The Discussion's explanation for the regional pattern -- better economic conditions aiding diagnosis of complex conditions -- is plausible, but it is offered as a substantive finding rather than as the confound it also is, and the limitations section does not mention site.

Two further things constrain what can be said. The abstract's four prevalence figures are not percentages of anything: no sample size between 2,700 and 2,900 makes all four whole-number counts, and 2,830 makes none of them one. They are the model's mixing proportions, which is legitimate, but they are presented as prevalences and they differ from the class sizes every test was actually run on -- by about 13% for the smallest class. And the model-selection statistics that justify four classes rather than three or five sit in a supplementary spreadsheet that exceeded the extraction limit, so the choice underpinning the entire analysis is the one step here that could not be checked at all.

The data availability statement is not a concern. Identifiable psychiatric inpatient records from three named hospitals carry a genuine ethical constraint, an approval number is given, and the paper does not claim the data are deposited when they are not.

This is a competently executed analysis with a real and serious internal-validity problem it does not acknowledge, sitting on a descriptive table that does not add up. The statistics that can be recalculated do recalculate. I would want the Table 1 definitions clarified, the medication associations reported within site, and the latent-class fit indices in the main text before treating the drug findings as anything more than hypothesis-generating.
